text:
objective: To simulate past and future forest cover changes in India using Land Change Modeler (LCM) and multi-layer perceptron neural network to understand spatio-temporal patterns of deforestation and afforestation.
country: India
land_use_classes: Forest; Non-Forest
baseline_years: 1880; 1930; 1975; 1985; 1995; 2005; 2013
target_future_years: 2025
scenarios: Business-as-usual (BAU)
analysis_methods: Land Change Modeler (LCM); Multi-layer perceptron (MLP) neural network; Markov-cellular automata (MCA) model; Change detection analysis; Transition potentials modelling; Cramer's V statistic for variable selection; Kappa statistic for validation
simulation_method_advantages: LCM considers driver data (e.g., proximity to roads, settlements) for spatial prediction, unlike Markov chain models which only give temporal dynamics. CA-Markov combines temporal and spatial pattern simulation, improving prediction accuracy.
predictors: Elevation; Slope; Distance to roads; Distance to settlements; Distance to water bodies
population_selected: Yes (population trends and growth mentioned as contextual factors influencing deforestation, but not used as a direct predictor variable in the model)
data_sources: Multi-temporal classified forest cover data from National Remote Sensing Centre (National Carbon Project); Historical archives (district and state level); Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) DEM; Forest cover maps from previous studies (Reddy et al. 2016a, b)
tools_software_used: IDRISI Selva software (Land Change Modeler)
validation_performed: Yes
validation_methods: Comparison of simulated forest cover map (2013) with actual classified forest cover map (2013); Computation of Cohen's Kappa statistic from confusion matrix
validation_data_sources: Actual remote sensing derived forest cover map for 2013
key_findings: Predicted forest cover in 1880 was 1,042,008 km² (31.7% of India); About 40% of forest cover lost between 1880–2013; Highest deforestation rates in Northeastern states and Andaman & Nicobar Islands (>0.3 annual gross rate from 2005–2013); Model predicted further decrease of 2305 km² of forest area in these regions by 2025; Majority of protected areas successful in protecting forest cover, except Manas, Sonai-Rupai, Nameri and Marat Longri; Deforestation rate greater during British rule (1880–1947) and early post-independence, decreased after 198s due to conservation policies; Inverse relationship between deforestation and elevation (low elevation forests more vulnerable); Slope and elevation were strongest explanatory variables for deforestation.
implications: Useful for effective resource management, biodiversity conservation, and climate change mitigation; Supports REDD+ Programme; Can aid in declaration of new protected areas and regional planning.
limitations: Model assumes business-as-usual scenario based on historical trends; Does not incorporate all socio-economic or political factors explicitly; Relies on accuracy of input historical and remote sensing data.
future_directions: Focus on vulnerable areas for effective conservation, enhancement of carbon stocks, and sustainable forest management.
scalability: Methodology can be applied to other regions for forest cover change modelling, given availability of multi-temporal land cover data and relevant spatial drivers.
novelty: Reconstruction of past forest cover (1880) using spatial modelling; Long-term (1880–2025) spatio-temporal prediction of forest cover changes at national scale; Integration of historical archives with remote sensing data and neural network modelling for India.
